reason: This passage from 2 Samuel 13-19 depicts a narrative of rebellion and civil conflict rather than presenting a model of good leadership. While Absalom strategically manipulates the people by promising better justice and governance (suggesting they valued functional government), his subsequent rebellion demonstrates how promises of superior governance are hollow when pursued through destructive means. The text does not present 'a functioning government to the benefit of the people' as an idealized model of good leadership. Instead, it focuses on political manipulation, family tragedy, and the chaos of civil war. David's leadership, while ultimately validated through military victory, is shown as flawed and incomplete in this passage—he flees his capital and grieves excessively over his rebellious son while neglecting to honor those who risked their lives defending his rule. The narrative is too complex and ambiguous to be read as endorsing any clear leadership model.
